newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Chernomyrdin survives yet another scare.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Chernomyrdin survives yet another scare.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin proved again on Tuesday that he is one of the great survivors of Russian politics by emerging smiling from yet another government reshuffle.

President Boris Yeltsin ignored the temptation to sack his stolid 58-year-old ally despite criticising his government's budget, its failure to pay wages and pensions, and its record on crime and tax collection.
Instead, Yeltsin gave Chernomyrdin -- together with reformer Anatoly Chubais -- an effectively free hand to form a new government.
The decision was a reward for Chernomyrdin's loyalty through more than four years as prime minister in which he has been almost constantly under fire in Russia over economic reforms.
Business circles both inside and outside Russia view him, however, as a guarantor of stability.

Above all, Chernomyrdin has been careful to avoid creating any impression that he is hungry to take over from Yeltsin, treading particularly carefully when the president has been out of the Kremlin with health problems.
"Chernomyrdin showed himself to be just as I expected -- solid and reliable. He did not let me down in a single critical or tough situation," Yeltsin wrote in his 1994 autobiography.
The stout, balding Chernomyrdin is viewed as a grey bureaucrat and many Russians blame him for the hardships they have endured under the reforms.

Critics say he lacks the charisma to be able to succeed Yeltsin as president, despite the backing of influential financial groups. Supporters say he would have a chance of winning an election if the state machinery united behind him.
He allowed television cameras a glimpse of his softer side last November, when he was filmed playing billiards, playing his piano accordion and dangling his grandson on his knee.

He even tasted glory for a day when Yeltsin had heart surgery last November and signed a decree transferring his powers temporarily to Chernomyrdin, briefly giving him charge of the trigger controlling Russia's nuclear arsenal.
Chernomyrdin is also widely known for his awkward, rambling mode of speech, which often lacks punctuation, and for his passion for hunting.

He provoked rare outrage in the Russian media in February for shooting dead two bear cubs and their mother, aroused from winter hibernation. Ogonyok magazine denounced his hunting expedition as "akin to common murder".
The premier was unrepentant. "I love hunting, I really love hunting, so it is with pleasure that I went when I had a free moment," he said.

Chernomyrdin's task had been to balance liberal requests for fast reforms with conservative demands for slower change Russian media say he has also worked out a way to avoid unneccessary confrontation with the opposition communists.
A former Communist Party member, he had won a reputation as an efficient manager as head of the state-owned natural gas monopoly Gazprom from 1989 until 1992.
But he surprised critics with his grim defence of reforms after his promotion to prime minister in December 1992 to replace reformer Yegor Gaidar.
He held on to his job despite a series of crises, including a brief but dramatic crash in the rouble's value in October 1994 which forced out several cabinet colleagues.

His government's tough monetary course has pushed down inflation but driven many companies close to bankruptcy. Taxes and wages go unpaid and millions of people struggle to survive on incomes well below the poverty line.

Chernomyrdin took a low profile in the early stages of Russia's military campaign in Chechnya but became more closely involved as Moscow started to seek peace, intervening to help end a hostage crisis in the southern Russian town of Budennovsk.

Chernomyrdin sailed through a confidence vote in the State Duma lower house of parliament soon after the Budennovsk raid and he hung on to power after the Communist Party made large gains in a parliamentary election in December 1995.
His centrist bloc, Our Home is Russia, won only just over 10 percent of the votes in the poll but is the second-largest party in the lower house after the communists.
Yeltsin renominated him as premier after the presidential election last July and parliament confirmed him in August.
Viktor Stepanovich Chernomyrdin, born on April 9, 1938, joined the Communist Party in 1961 and worked his way up to join the Central Committee's industry department. He left the party in 1991.
He worked in Russia's main oil-producing region, Tyumen, in western Siberia, from 1983 to 1985 and became gas industry minister in 1985 under Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.
He is married with two grown-up daughters and a son.
